examples.question_text:
The table gives three values of a function.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&2&5&8\\\hline f(x)&4&7&6\end{array}$
Approximate $\int_2^8 f(x)\,dx$ by adding two trapezium areas. Then check using the composite Trapezoidal rule.
examples.solution_text:
Three ordinates give two strips.
$\begin{aligned}h&=\frac{8-2}{2}\\&=3\end{aligned}$
Add the two trapezium areas.
$\begin{aligned}T&=\frac{3}{2}(4+7)+\frac{3}{2}(7+6)\\&=16.5+19.5\\&=36\end{aligned}$
The interior ordinate belongs to both trapeziums, so it is counted twice.
$\begin{aligned}\int_2^8 f(x)\,dx&\approx\frac{3}{2}[4+6+2(7)]\\&=36\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Use the Trapezoidal rule with two strips and then four strips to approximate $\int_0^2\frac{1}{1+x}\,dx$. Give each estimate to three decimal places. The exact value is $\ln3\approx1.099$. Which estimate is closer? Explain why both estimates exceed the exact value.
Use three strips to approximate $\int_0^3(9-x^2)\,dx$. Find the exact value and explain geometrically why the trapezoidal estimate is smaller.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}h&=\frac{3-0}{3}\\&=1\end{aligned}$
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}x&0&1&2&3\\\hline f(x)&9&8&5&0\end{array}$
$\begin{aligned}T&=\frac12[9+0+2(8+5)]\\&=17.5\end{aligned}$
The exact integral is
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_0^3(9-x^2)\,dx\\&=\left[9x-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3\\&=27-9\\&=18.\end{aligned}$
For $f(x)=9-x^2$,
$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=-2x\\f''(x)&=-2.\end{aligned}$
The curve is concave down. Each chord lies below the curve, so the trapeziums miss some area and $17.5<18$.

examples.question_text: Use two strips to approximate the signed integral $\int_0^2(x^2-6)\,dx$. Use concavity to compare the estimate with the exact integral. What does this imply for the estimated unsigned area between the curve and the $x$-axis?
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}h&=\frac{2-0}{2}\\&=1\end{aligned}$
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&0&1&2\\\hline f(x)&-6&-5&-2\end{array}$
$\begin{aligned}T&=\frac12[-6-2+2(-5)]\\&=-9\end{aligned}$
Since $f''(x)=2>0$, the curve is concave up and its chords lie above it. The signed estimate is therefore greater than the exact integral, even though both are negative.
The graph lies below the axis throughout the interval. Negating the signed estimate gives an unsigned area estimate of $9$ square units, which is smaller than the true area.

examples.question_text:
An object has positive velocity throughout the first six seconds. Its measured velocities are shown below.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}t\text{ (s)}&0&2&4&6\\\hline v\text{ (m/s)}&1.8&2.6&3.4&4.2\end{array}$
Distance travelled is the area under the velocity/time graph. Use the Trapezoidal rule to estimate this distance.
examples.solution_text:
The measurements are two seconds apart, so $h=2$.
$\begin{aligned}d&\approx\frac22[1.8+4.2+2(2.6+3.4)]\\&=6+12\\&=18\text{ m}.\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text:
a. A lake's widths are measured at ten-metre intervals along a straight survey line. Estimate its surface area.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}x\text{ (m)}&0&10&20&30&40\\\hline \text{width (m)}&0&16&22&18&0\end{array}$
b. A vertical rock cutting has a straight horizontal base. Its heights are measured at thirty-metre intervals. Estimate its area.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}x\text{ (m)}&0&30&60&90\\\hline \text{height (m)}&3&7&8&4\end{array}$
examples.solution_text:
a. Use the measured widths as ordinates, with $h=10$.
$\begin{aligned}A&\approx\frac{10}{2}[0+0+2(16+22+18)]\\&=5(112)\\&=560\text{ m}^2.\end{aligned}$
b. Use the measured heights as ordinates, with $h=30$.
$\begin{aligned}A&\approx\frac{30}{2}[3+4+2(7+8)]\\&=15(37)\\&=555\text{ m}^2.\end{aligned}$

examples.derivation: Two strips give h=3. Individual contributions are 3(4+7)/2=16.5 and 3(7+6)/2=19.5, totalling 36. The composite calculation is 3[4+6+2(7)]/2=36. Matches booklet Foundation Q2.

For two strips, T2=[1+1/3+2(1/2)]/2=7/6≈1.167. For four strips, T4=[1+1/3+2(2/3+1/2+2/5)]/4=67/60≈1.117. Their errors relative to ln(3) are approximately 0.068054 and 0.018054. Since f''=2/(1+x)^3>0, both overestimate. The plotted curve, ordinates and four green chords agree with these values. Methods match the reciprocal investigation and concavity teaching.

With h=1, ordinates are 9,8,5,0, giving T=[9+0+2(8+5)]/2=17.5. Independently integrating gives [9x-x^3/3] from 0 to 3=18. Since f''=-2, chords lie below the curve and the estimate is smaller. Matches Foundation Q5's exact-versus-trapezoidal comparison. The bare integral has the required phantom relation gutter.

With h=1 and ordinates -6,-5,-2, T=[-6-2+2(-5)]/2=-9. The exact integral is [x^3/3-6x] from 0 to 2=-28/3. Thus -9>-28/3. The graph remains negative and f''=2>0, so the estimated unsigned area 9 is smaller than the true area 28/3. Supported by negative-ordinate trapezoidal teaching, signed-area conventions and the retained accepted assessment method.
The time spacing is 2 seconds. The distance estimate is 2[1.8+4.2+2(2.6+3.4)]/2=18 metres. Positive velocity permits interpreting the integral as distance. Matches Development Q9.

Lake: h=10 and full-width ordinates give 10[0+0+2(16+22+18)]/2=560 square metres. Cutting: h=30 gives 30[3+4+2(7+8)]/2=555 square metres. Both tables have the correct column counts. The supplied source images confirm full lake widths and cutting heights as the respective ordinates. Matches Development Q10–Q11.

With h=0.5, ordinates are 2,√15/2,√3,√7/2,0. Their trapezoidal combination is (2+√15+2√3+√7)/4≈2.995709068, rounding to 2.9957. The exact quarter-circle area is π because the radius is 2, yielding π≈3.0 to one decimal place. The circle is concave down, so the estimate is too small. The circular arc, chord endpoints, vertical strips and purposeful shading are consistent. Matches Development Q12.
